title: The BRCK: A Router Sketched on a Flight Home for Nairobi's Blackouts
dek: A side project begun on a dull flight became a rugged Kenyan router built to keep working when the power and the internet went out.

story.founder: Erik Hersman, Juliana Rotich, Reg Orton, Philip Walton
story.event: Designing and prototyping the BRCK backup router in Nairobi and launching it on Kickstarter
story.summary: Erik Hersman sketched a router for African conditions on a flight from South Africa to Kenya (dated in a later interview to November 2011) as a side project for Ushahidi's team, who suffered frequent power and internet cuts in Nairobi. Self-funded by Ushahidi and prototyped in California and Nairobi, the BRCK, with eight hours of battery and 3G failover, was announced in May 2013 and raised $172,107 from 1,078 Kickstarter backers; the first 800 units had shipped to 45 countries by August 2014.
paragraphs: On 6 May 2013 Erik Hersman was in Berlin, finishing a talk for re:publica, as a post went up on his blog announcing a small black box called the BRCK. The idea, he wrote, had come on a flight from South Africa back to Kenya, with no book and his phone nearly flat; a 2014 interview dates that flight to November 2011. Bored, he opened a notebook and sketched what he thought would be "a fun hardware side-project" for Ushahidi's core team, something to turn to when they were too tired for their usual coding.

The problem was their own. Even in Nairobi, with four undersea cables, he wrote, "we still have power and connectivity problems," and for a web company small outages rippled through everything. Members of the iHub, the Nairobi tech space he had founded in 2010, were getting round failures with 3G dongles. Juliana Rotich, Ushahidi's executive director, told a TED audience the routine: the power cuts out, the internet goes with it, and you go looking for the modem. "Blackouts are not fun," she said.

Ushahidi had only ever made software, and local finance, Rotich said, did not back hardware. The team started from Hersman's question: "How would we design a redundant internet device for Africa?" It had to run eight hours without mains power, fall back to 3G when the cable failed, work in any country with a change of SIM card, and stay open to other people's add-ons. Jon Shuler made early builds in California, which Hersman carried to Nairobi for Brian Muita to work on the firmware. By the fifth prototype they were milling bodies at the University of Nairobi's FabLab, after a couple of days of repairs to its machine. Reg Orton became the electrical and mechanical engineer of the first release, Philip Walton its first software engineer. Ushahidi paid for the research itself.

A Kickstarter campaign asked for $125,000 towards production; 1,078 backers pledged $172,107. Refining it for production took about another year. Orton said building in Nairobi, slow as it was, was "the best way to understand the real problems and challenges that the BRCK is here to solve." By August 2014 the first 800 units, at $199 each, had shipped to 45 countries.

quote.text: One that reckoneth accounts all the day passeth not an happy moment. One that gladdeneth his heart all the day provideth not for his house. The bowman hitteth the mark, as the steersman reacheth land, by diversity of aim.
quote.work: The Instruction of Ptahhotep (and of Ke'gemni)
quote.source_title: The Instruction of Ptah-Hotep and the Instruction of Ke'Gemni, tr. Battiscombe G. Gunn, Project Gutenberg eBook #30508
quote.connection: Gunn read the steersman as a sailor tacking, and the maxim as a case for alternating work and play. The BRCK came from exactly such a change of course: a bored hour on a plane and a side project for a team too tired for its usual work.

reflection: When you are worn out, the instinct is to push harder at the same task. Hersman's team did something else: they gave tired people a different kind of problem, one they lived with every day. The router came out of that change of aim, and out of an hour with nothing to do.

You do not have to turn your tired hours into anything. But the times when your phone is flat and nothing is asked of you are not wasted, and a nuisance you meet every week, at work or at home, may be worth sketching rather than only putting up with.
invitation: Leave your phone in another room for twenty minutes today with a notebook beside you. Write down one small frustration that keeps coming back, and sketch, roughly, what would make it go away.

research_notes: Distinct from the seed edition on Ushahidi's first six days (January 2008): this is the 2011-2013 design of a hardware product, though Hersman and Rotich appear in both. Date of the idea: Hersman's post of 6 May 2013 says the flight was 'a year ago'; Business Daily (2014) dates it to November 2011; Quartz (May 2013, blocked for the checker) said 'more than a year ago'. The story gives Hersman's account and Business Daily's date, attributed. First production run: MIT Technology Review (May 2013) said Kickstarter would fund 1,000 units; TechCentral (May 2013) said 2,000 units in Shenzhen; Business Daily (August 2014) reported the first 800 units shipped. The story gives only the shipped figure, from Business Daily, with its date. Kickstarter total: Business Daily gives $172,107 from 1,078 backers; Vice rounds to $172,000; the story uses Business Daily's figure. Price: Business Daily $199, TechCentral about $200; the story uses $199. Founders: CrazyEngineers names Hersman, Orton and Walton as co-founders; Vice calls Rotich a BRCK co-founder and Orton CTO; Hersman's May 2013 post names neither Orton nor Walton among the early builders (Shuler, Muita), so the story places Orton and Walton on the first release, as CrazyEngineers does. Rotich's TED account of looking for the modem is paraphrased; her quoted words are exact from the TED transcript. Hersman's own blog domain no longer serves the post, so the Internet Archive copy (January 2014 capture) is cited, with a later repost on Ventureburn. Funding is 'mixed' at the time of the episode: Ushahidi (a nonprofit) self-funded the research and the first production was crowdfunded; BRCK later raised angel and venture money (Ken Banks mentions crowdfunding and angel investors), which falls outside this episode. The Ptahhotep maxim's reading as alternating work and play is Gunn's own footnote.
